title: Guards must accept what the question asks
statement: Every rule that can refuse an answer must accept one that does exactly what the question asks, so test it on the wanted answer in its expected words.
example: A copying rule rejected word-perfect recall because the sentence made up 84/114 = 0.74 of a marking criterion, over its 0.70 threshold.
detail: A fragment rule gave no credit to the short phrase a question asked for, so a student who did exactly what the stem said, quote a short phrase, scored nothing and was told to say the whole idea as one full sentence (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-course/ADVERSARIAL-REVIEW-2026-09-16-R25.md`). A rubric edit that dropped the phrase a fragment rule keyed on would have refused one-word answers until a test caught it, and one blank carried acceptance rules that disagreed with each other (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-inceptbench-2026-09-30/REGISTER.md`). A copying check counted the marking criteria as text a student could copy, so on three recall pages word-perfect recall was rejected, the sentence making up 84/114 = 0.74 of a criterion against a 0.70 threshold (`grade3-reading/artifacts/build-closing-questions-2026-09-25/verify/DIGEST.md`); a later validator rule holds that a criterion states the standard and does not quote the story (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-course/ADVERSARIAL-REVIEW-2026-09-16-R26.md`). Such rules include fragment and copying rules. Keep any recall target short enough to pass a copying rule, and let a copying rule count only text the student was shown.
against: The fragment rule's harm was bounded, since a student who then gave the phrase with an explanation passed: "Not CRITICAL because the child who then" (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-course/ADVERSARIAL-REVIEW-2026-09-16-R25.md`, line 53).
